item.title: [amitseg] Historically, in manual primary elections, turnout stands at around 50–55 percent. In the Labor Party, it used to reach
item.description:
Open
Historically, in manual primary elections, turnout stands at around 50–55 percent. In the Labor Party, it used to reach 60–70 percent during the good old days of Fuad, often due to fraud.

With digital voting, like the system used by the Democrats, turnout rises to 85 percent or even higher.

Historically, Netanyahu was very concerned about cyberattacks. He had in mind the possibility of a foreign country interfering in order to sabotage the party list.

After the 2022 elections, he became convinced that the process was secure. The more people who vote, the weaker the influence of organized blocs controlled by figures such as Bitan and Haim Katz.

So why didn’t it happen this time? My guess is that Netanyahu’s problem this time is actually the independent voters. Tally Gotliv, for example, doesn’t appear in the vote-dealing arrangements, but she is strong among individual party members. By contrast, in return for reserving Haim Katz a spot on the list, Netanyahu got Katz’s people included in the major Israel Aerospace Industries voting deal.

I still think that if Likud opened up its ranks and adopted digital voting, it could attract hundreds of thousands of voters—outsiders who have no interest in selling their souls in exchange for a political deal—and end up with a much better slate than the one that will probably be elected tonight.

My husband, Shlomo, served in the reserves recovering bodies at Camp Shura. He has already served more than 700 days of reserve duty. At Camp Shura, he was exposed to things no human being should ever have to see, and episodes of shock and panic strike him almost every night.

We started a fundraising campaign to give Shlomo—and especially our family—some breathing room, so that we don’t collapse under the financial burden and the debts that have accumulated.
